alt: Four parts of 3.2.2 with printed title and actual content. 3.2.2.1 Individuals and Society covers culture and the sociological imagination; 3.2.2.2 Socialisation, highlighted, is this guide; 3.2.2.3, titled Social Identities and Social Change, actually covers social control; 3.2.2.4, titled Social Control, actually covers crime and deviance.
caption: The titles of 3.2.2.3 and 3.2.2.4 are crossed, so cite part numbers and contents.

alt: A life-course line. Primary socialisation happens early, mainly in the family; secondary socialisation follows through wider agencies; re-socialisation replaces earlier norms after a major life change. Four cards define primary, secondary, re-socialisation and inadequate socialisation, which some perspectives link to later deviance.
caption: Know all four types as separate concepts, not just primary and secondary.

alt: Six agencies around the individual. Family socialises through direct instruction and role modelling; school through the formal and hidden curriculum; media through modelling behaviours in its content. Peers, religion and the workplace are left for students to complete with their own process.
caption: Name the agency and the process: listing agencies alone loses marks.

alt: Left: three structural views. Functionalists see socialisation as necessary for order and consensus; Marxists see the ruling class reproducing its dominance; feminists see gender roles reproduced through family and media. Right: the social action or interactionist view, in which individuals interpret, negotiate and sometimes resist norms.
caption: Three perspectives see socialisation shaping people; interactionists see people shaping it.

after: ## Worked example: comparing two perspectives on socialisation
alt: Side by side: functionalists see socialisation instilling shared values for a smoothly running society; Marxists see the bourgeoisie instilling obedience and acceptance of inequality, with schools reproducing class inequality. A note says to finish with an explicit point of contrast.
caption: A compare answer states both views, then names the difference.

alt: Two pairs of terms. Values are broad beliefs about what is important; norms are the specific unwritten rules of behaviour. An agency is who socialises, such as family, school or media; a process is how, such as role modelling. Below, identity is socially constructed through interaction with agencies.
caption: Values are beliefs, norms are rules; an agency is who, a process is how.
